title: Efteling sets opening date for new Raveleijn area, Ravenring attraction
summary:
Efteling, the fairytale theme park in the Netherlands, has announced an opening date for its new Raveleijn themed area.

From 1 December, guests will get to experience the renovated Raveleijn area, watch the new Raveleijn: Battle for the City stunt show, and enjoy the new Ravenring attraction.

Additionally, the revamped themed area will include updated F&B facilities and a new souvenir shop.

Efteling has invested a total of €20 million in the new Raveleijn themed area – €10m in the show, €5m in the area's renovation, and €5m in the new Ravenring attraction.

Starting with the new show, Efteling's director of product, marketing and image, Koen Sanders, said the sets have been "extensively revamped".

Raveleijn: Battle for the City, he added, is "packed with spectacular stunts, created in collaboration with the French theme park Puy du Fou".

Efteling, the fairytale theme park in the Netherlands, has announced an opening date for its new Raveleijn themed areaEfteling

As for the new Ravenring attraction, riders will soar through the air in one of 18 winged vehicles inspired by ravens, using levers to tilt themselves.

Efteling said Ravenring "is a completely new attraction" developed by Vekoma Rides, the Dutch roller coaster specialist.

The Raveleijn area's revamped F&B offering is called De Verslaeghen Draek Inn, and the new shop is named In den Ravenkorf.

See on Instagram

Earlier this summer, Efteling announced plans for its newest thrill ride – a suspended launch coaster called Missie Luminar set to open in 2029.

The park later shared a first look at its 32nd fairytale – 'The Fairytale Library'.

title: Preparing the world's theme parks for the next generation
summary:
One of the things I love about the theme park industry is that it is always growing, evolving and changing. On one hand, this keeps the park offerings fresh and new and helps keep up with the latest technical innovations and concepts dreamed up each year by various manufacturers.

The other side of the coin is less obvious, but just as essential. This means growing and evolving your park to keep pace not only with what consumers want right now, but also with broader societal trends.

This includes keeping close tabs not only on what each generation and demographic deems popular at any given moment, but also on things that may have fallen out of favor.

Or even worse… things that were once acceptable that have now been decided are actually now in bad taste or something deemed to be racist, insensitive or offensive.

Examples of the latter kind have come up far more often than you might think over the years, especially when it comes to offensive and even racist depictions in theme parks as they age.

Updating outdated themes

Even Disney faced issues. A few years ago, it retired Splash Mountain, a popular E-Ticket ride, because modern audiences found its “southern" portrayals offensive. The ride was based on The Song of the South (1946), a film rarely released in full due to racism concerns.

A scene from Tiana's Bayou Adventure at Walt Disney World, a retheme of Splash Mountain

Opened in 1988, Splash Mountain was initially seen as free of such issues. However, Disney later decided to retire the theme, replacing it with a new story based on The Princess and the Frog, debuting in 2024.

Disney has modified attractions multiple times, including scene changes in Jungle Cruise where character animatronics like ‘Trader Sam’ have been altered or removed over the years as public opinion changed.

The various changes over the years to the Pirates of the Caribbean attractions have also been well documented regarding the treatment of women that did not age well.

Such changes are common and not unique to Disney.

Several European parks have also changed how various cultural figures are depicted over time, as part of periodic updates to the attractions. Some did so in response to complaints, while others simply recognised that times had changed and proactively updated them without drawing media attention.

Rides for the whole family

While old stereotypes have mostly been erased, the global attractions industry has always evolved alongside changing guest expectations.

Looking back, every generation has redefined what constitutes a memorable day at a theme park, from the golden age of amusement parks to the transformation into theme parks, and from the rise of blockbuster roller coaster thrills never before imagined to the emergence of immersive themed lands and destination resorts.

See also: Beyond the kiddie coaster

Today, even as the industry is in the middle of one change, we are also approaching another pivotal moment when things will have to evolve again to appease the next generation.

NightFlight Expedition is the largest attraction investment in the history of Dollywood Parks & Resorts

On one end of the spectrum, I’ve previously mentioned how parks have already started to adjust their offering to appease a population base of dedicated theme park fans that are just getting older.

They may not be as attracted to hard-core thrill rides as they were in their youth, but as a generation that grew up visiting theme parks, they still come to visit and often bring along children and their grandchildren. As such, I already see increased demand for multi-generational attractions.

So while the time may not be right for a roller coaster with 10 inversions, it may be the perfect time for something new and unique, like a custom dark ride experience that guests of all ages can enjoy, such as NightFlight Expedition at Dollywood.

New versions of much-loved attractions

If a beloved attraction has reached the point of being retired, then it is possible to build an all-new version of it for the next generation, as Silver Dollar City did in 2024 when it opened a brand new version of Fire in the Hole.

Knott’s Berry Farm has also spent much of the last 15 years either building new attractions based on lost classics, like 2021’s Knott’s Bear-y Tales: Return to the Fair dark ride, or taking efforts to update and preserve classics like the Calico Mine Ride and Timber Mountain Log Ride.

Engaging a new generation of fans: the return of Knott’s Bear-y Tales

And after a 4-year renovation, the park will reopen the closed Montezooma’s Revenge shuttle coaster as Montezooma: The Forbidden Fortress this month.

This last effort is kind of a fun one to think about as well: instead of being a dark ride, “Monty” is a classic 1978 Schwarzkopf Shuttle Loop coaster.

However, the design is far from extreme and as classic as you can get, with the original ride design upgraded to offer new theming, new trains, and a modern-style magnetic launch and braking system.

Going forward, for current and future generations, Montezuma will still serve the very important purpose of being a fantastic introduction for younger riders to experience their first roller coaster inversion.

The great thing is that while the thrill is still fun, it isn’t so extreme that a parent or grandparent couldn’t ride along with the child, making it a memorable option for families of all ages to experience together.

What do Gen Z and Gen Alpha want from a park experience?

So the question now is… what should we expect from future generations?

The next generation of park visitors will be led by “Generation Alpha” (born between 2012 and 2024) along with the younger half of “Generation Z” (born between 1997 and 2012).

Technology has been a key defining factor in the lives of both generations, with Gen Z being the first to grow up with the internet and the knowledge and changes it brought to the world. They were also the generation to see the birth of the smartphone from early childhood, connecting their world to the internet at all times.

Another major influence on Gen Z is that most of them had parents who fell firmly into the infamous Gen X demographic (1965 - 1980), the generation that grew up around the big theme park boom of those years.

So, it stands to reason that Gen-X parents not only took their Gen-Z kids to visit theme parks often, but there's also a good chance they are still visiting and starting to take their grandchildren as well.

Gen Z are digital natives, and technology plays a key role in their lives and experiences

This brings us to the Generation Alpha kids, who have been surrounded by technology from birth.

They were probably given tablets to play with or be entertained by as infants, had their own smartphones before finishing elementary school, and grew up being able to stream video content on an as-needed basis rather than waiting for a show to come at a certain time.

They had access to video games, social media, and the rise of smart speakers with artificial intelligence-driven answers to nearly any question they could dream of asking.

Because they have instant access to information or content of any kind at all times, their expectations of how things work, especially in terms of entertainment, are fundamentally different from those of all previous generations.

In their world, “Google” isn’t just a brand; it's become a verb, and one they leaned into heavily during periods of isolation in the pandemic years, when staying at home was the norm.

According to studies, Gen Alphas value participation over simple observation, personalised experiences over a one-size-fits-all approach, and meaningful experiences over generic ones.

For theme parks, zoos, aquariums, FECs, attractions, museums, and even resorts, understanding the next generation of customers will be more of a challenge. The attractions that thrive over the next decade may not be the ones that spent extra to build the tallest, fastest, or longest new rides.

Instead, your success may depend far more on how well you understand how this generation thinks, interacts, and what concepts they will base their purchasing choices on.

Interactivity and personalisation

As mentioned, this is a generation born and raised on the concept of interactivity. Remember, this was the generation that didn’t sit and wait for the TV shows they wanted to see to come to them on a schedule; instead, they could stream and binge-watch whole series at the touch of a button.

Gen Alpha grew up with media apps that not only remembered what they had watched, but also used algorithms to suggest new programs they might like to watch next.

Video games are increasingly influencing theme park design

The video games they grew up playing are not just simple side-scrollers taken on a linear path. Instead, today's games often feature different outcomes that reveal themselves based on players' choices.

Open-world gaming concepts are the norm, and some of the best experiences are had through multiplayer. As a result, Gen Alpha will increasingly expect their entertainment to evolve in response to their own actions, likes, and dislikes.

This shift in attitude will have significant implications for attraction design. While mechanical ride systems will always be essential for parks and attractions, guests will increasingly seek experiences that let them be active participants rather than passive spectators.

They will want to see this need met not only on the attraction itself, but also in the queue. This can take the form of character encounters and storytelling, gamified challenges or missions played out possibly via mobile devices, and more.

Disney and Universal rise to the challenge

I would say that the newly introduced version of the Millennium Falcon: Smuggler’s Run at Disneyland and Walt Disney World would very much be in response to this concept. At its heart, the attraction is built like a giant video game.

Thanks to the latest version that just opened a few months ago, Smuggler’s Run now features three different possible missions you can embark on, each with its own unique outcome, along with different tasks to perform along the way, depending on which seat/station you are manning during the adventure.

It is a great start, and much like how we’ve seen new additions to Star Tours over the years, I think we will continue to see this attraction grow and expand with even more missions as time goes on.

Universal has also been tackling the same sort of concept, but in a different way, offering an expanding series of interactive elements across its themed lands, especially at the new Epic Universe park.

Animatronic monster in Dark Universe at Universal Epic Universe

Each land offers a different form of interactivity that would appeal to Gen Alpha and Gen Z guests.

The Isle of Berk has created a very visually diverse land full of different dragons and characters to interact with, as well as featuring some of the park’s more physically demanding attractions.

Epic’s new extension into The Wizarding World of Harry Potter continues the tradition of interactive stations where guests can engage with the world by purchasing a Magic Wand.

Dark Universe has quite literally brought the world of the Universal Monsters to life in a way that is both very exploratory as well as interactive, thanks to the use of a variety of live-action characters that can be found as you explore the world.

Finally, we have Super Nintendo World, where guests can purchase a wristband that not only allows them to interact with the entire video game-like world itself, but also syncs with a mobile app to track and score how they play, not only on the first visit, but also on future visits, so they can continue to grow their experience level.

Being themed to the world of Nintendo in general, you know the level and extent of the gameplay just had to be next level, with interactive moments not just spread throughout the land, but into the restaurants, shops, attractions and even the queues as well.

Embracing innovation

Clearly, we can already see early adopters responding to the needs of future guests by designing attractions that encourage exploration and discovery, not just pushing them through a queue into a predetermined narrative.

Parks will need to keep creating new environments where visitors can influence their experience through the choices they make and the actions they take.

And yet… even this might not be enough if the number of choices or end results becomes stagnant.

This is where the rise of AI in theme park environments can come into play, helping keep parts of the experience evolving over time, even when budgets may not allow for full rebuilds or updates.

Millennium Falcon: Smuggler's Run allows visitors to influence the experience

Even after the guests return home, a digital platform could continue to reach out to communicate and engage with guests, both extending the “story”, perhaps to provide in-park photo links for social media posts, or online games that may offer some kind of reward redemption for points.

Even more important, continued engagement with guests can generate links and reminders for future return-trip planning.

Park and attraction operators that embrace innovation while still remaining focused on creating truly authentic guest experiences will be well positioned to thrive in this increasingly competitive marketplace.

However, in the end, the most successful attractions may simply be the ones that have come to understand the simplest of truths.

Guests may not always remember exactly what they did or everything they saw, but they will remember who they went with and how the experience made them feel.

title: Driving innovative attraction design: the what-if and why of blue sky thinking
summary:
The Designing attractions: innovation in blue sky session at the Festival of Innovation featured guest speakers Henry Kim, creative director at Forrec, and Virginie Valastro, producer at Moment Factory.

In discussion with blooloop’s managing director, Ella Baskerville, they explored what blue sky thinking means, where to begin when designing an attraction or experience and how to future-proof ideas.


  • Defining blue sky thinking. The speakers describe the blue sky mindset as "what if," where creative ideas are given time to exist and develop before being constrained by operational or technological "how" factors.
  • The role of technology. Technology should serve as an invisible layer that supports storytelling and emotional connection rather than driving the design process; overreliance on tech can sometimes detract from the magic of an experience.
  • Future-proofing through timeless drivers. To design for the long term, creators should focus on timeless human drivers, such as curiosity, connection, and agency, rather than trying to future-proof against rapidly changing technology.
  • Personalisation and engagement. Successful attractions of the future will rely on personalisation and discovery, where guests are active participants or "co-authors" of the story, rather than passive observers.
  • The wellness opportunity. There is significant, untapped growth potential in the wellness sector, where designers can move beyond traditional spectacle and adrenaline to create spaces focused on calm, restoration, and emotional recharge.

The Festival of Innovation took place online from 21 to 22 January 2026 and celebrated the creative ideas, products, and organisations advancing the attractions sector.

The winners of the blooloop Innovation Awards Blue Sky category were announced during the session. First place went to The Giant, with AccesPro from Etholle Holmes in second place and Proviva’s ‘Magic Carpet’ awarded third.

The world’s tallest moving 3D human-shaped statue, The Giant is an LED-covered fusion of art, technology, commerce and interactive storytelling

The blooloop Innovation Awards, held in partnership with Area15, recognise the remarkable energy, creativity, and imagination that propel the attractions industry forward.

Submissions for the 2026 awards are now open.

Meet the speakers

Henry Kim is a creative director at FORREC, a Toronto-based experience design company serving clients across the world.

His portfolio includes the Three Kingdoms Theme Park in Hangzhou, Six Flags Chongqing, LEGOLAND Shanghai Resort, and the Babylon Hotel & Resort in Vietnam.

Designing attractions: innovation in blue sky at the Festival of Innovation featuring speakers Henry Kim and Virginie Valastro

Virginie Valastro has 25 years of experience in the entertainment sector, spanning a wide range of storytelling media. She has worked with some of North America’s leading companies as production manager, line producer, associate producer, and producer.

Valastro's understanding of creative and production processes enables her to deliver engaging projects in immersive environments. Her work at Moment Factory has included complex work with cutting-edge technologies on non-traditional large-scale media canvases.

‘What if’

This session sought to explore the challenge of designing at the vanguard of attractions and how concepts that look some five or 10 years into the future can also be future-proofed.

To kick off the discussion, Baskerville asked what the term ‘blue sky’ means to each of the guest speakers.

For both, the term reflects a sense of ‘what if’.

“I think blue sky means different things to different people,” says Kim.

“It can mean out-of-the-box thinking, chasing that elusive big idea, or really, the initial spark of an idea.

“But for me, I've always thought that it's a mindset; it's really deliberately spending time in the realm of what if. Before letting the ‘how’ slow the idea down.”

Forrec contributed to the concept master plan, schematic design, and design development of Legoland Shanghai Resort

“To me,” he adds, “a blue sky mindset really means giving those ideas the time and permission to exist long enough to see where they might take us.”

“On our side,” says Valastro, “multimedia often resonates with technology, and so we like to think of technology, how it's meant to be used, and just think how it could be used differently.”

Technology as tools

Baskerville then asked if the speakers could share examples of where they begin when designing an experience.

Kim says that blue sky thinking can occur at any stage of the development process. For instance, Forrec joined Legoland Shanghai after the earliest concept phase.

“Blue sky thinking allowed us to think about how families play together, how they move through the space, and what moments of wonder really, truly resonate,” says Kim.

“And from there we could really begin the groundwork, start thinking about the brand, site operations, and really turn it into something both authentic and buildable.”

Valastro agrees that understanding the context is key. This includes emotional and cultural landmarks, and should be both specific to the destination and broader in scope.

Curiosity Cove at Mandai Wildlife Reserve is Singapore's largest nature-inspired indoor playscape for children aged 3 to 12Image courtesy of Moment Factory

Developed over eight years, she notes how Curiosity Cove offered the opportunity to rethink and refine.

“Where are we at? What are we creating, and where do we want to bring it? Is it still the right purpose, the right emotion that we're bringing to the table? And what are the tools that we're using?

“We really see technology as a tool to service the emotion. And so, once we really have a strong idea and a strong story, then it's just seeing what tools are there to elevate it.”

The panel emphasises that it's not about using the newest technologies or anticipating upcoming releases. Technologies are selected, repurposed and revisited to support the story.

Balanced approach to blue sky

The conversation then turned to when blue sky needs to consider operational realities.

“Operations absolutely, always matter,” says Kim. “You can't design a park that's never going to run safely or efficiently.”

But, he adds, “If you bring operations in too soon, you risk running down ideas before they've had time to grow.

“The key is timing. Once the big idea is clear, operations can become a creative partner.”

An example is the queue line. Once considered a constraint, they are now viewed as part of the experience, layering in interactive storytelling and immersive environments.

“Constraints like these can actually help push us to create solutions that are both elegant and memorable, as well as efficient.”

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by FORREC (@forrecdesigns)

Valastro highlights the need for balance. While operations may force creativity, an awareness of where they can also throttle ideas is key.

So, Baskerville asked, are there planning assumptions that have potential for reinvention?

Kim sees dwell time shifting from a capacity metric to become part of the experience itself, for example, making crush spaces interactive and layered.

Guest flow also presents opportunities as designers look beyond efficient movement to enhancing discovery and anticipation.

At Moment Factory, guests’ diminishing attention spans are being considered.

“We constantly have to ask ourselves, even if this scene is four minutes or 10 minutes, is it too long, will we lose our guests' attention?” says Valastro.

“We have to find that balance of what will keep them engaged, for them to fully enjoy and appreciate the experience.”

Personalised and collective

Once you have the experience, how do you get guests to repeat?

Kim says that personalisation and discovery are what “turn experience into something deeper, something worth repeating.”

These qualities, he adds, enable guests to shape their own experience and become active participants.

For Valastro, repeatability hinges on the type of experience being delivered.

For passive engagement, where spectators are watching a show or media, this might be seasonal content. Whereas interactive experiences can encourage repeats through gamified, competitive layers.

Halloween events draw huge crowds and boost seasonal profits in the themed entertainment industry

And to what extent are both organisations using AI to deliver personalisation?

“Technology shouldn't be driving,” says Kim. “Whether it's brainstorming or the development and planning, AI is always a tool for me.”

At Moment Factory, a dedicated department is learning how to train AI for positive use within the sector. However, Valastro adds that AI needs to be deployed selectively and often cannot deliver work of the same refined quality as human artists.

The panellists shared other emerging technologies that they find exciting.

Kim is anticipating advances that quietly adapt experiences in real time, without calling attention to themselves.

This could be technology that senses pace or mood, for example, and subtly responds through lighting, sound, and spatial changes. Ultimately, this enhances personalisation and immersion.

Valastro is curious about technology that helps foster collective experiences and extends the experience before and after the visit.

She envisages quests that take guests to other attractions, or real-life meetups for the attraction’s community.

Wellness as opportunity

Considering different verticals, Baskerville asked whether there are any notable, less-traditional theme park experiences showing significant growth.

“Wellness is dramatically unexplored,” says Kim.

“Our industry has spent a lot of time focusing on adrenaline and spectacle, but what we haven't done is design enough for calm and reflection, and an emotional recharge.”

High-stress, emotionally charged environments like airports and transit spaces, he adds, present opportunities to create moments of surprise and delight through storytelling and thoughtful placement.

“I think the industry has only started to scratch the surface in these spaces.”

Valastro says that Moment Factory’s distinct market units offer an advantage by enabling idea sharing across verticals such as transportation hubs, outdoor nighttime experiences, and brand experiences.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by MOMENT FACTORY (@momentfactory)

“We are lucky to be exploring all of these canvases and markets already, and so sharing that information, or those discoveries, or those tests that we're doing, prototyping, and cross-contaminating the different sectors.”

Additionally, she agrees with Kim that wellness is under-exploited.

“We have broken the barriers a little bit with Aquascope. Integrating multimedia into the water world was quite a challenge, but it proved a very successful outcome, appreciated by both visitors and the industry.

“I think we're approaching that area with a lot more confidence now, thinking what the possibilities could be.”

Emerging trends

The conversations then looked ahead to the next decade. What will be the most successful attraction of the next decade? And what key factors will define success?

Both panellists feel that co-authorship will be key over the coming years.

“I think really the future belongs to experiences that feel personal,” says Kim.

“The most successful attractions won't be about technology or scale. I think they will be layers to it, but it's really about how deeply it connects with each guest.”

For Kim, experiences need to be co-authored by the guests, rather than just delivered to them, such as Punchdrunk’s Sleep No More.

Punchdrunk's immersive theatre production Sleep No More blurs the lines between audience and participant

“I think that kind of personal engagement is exactly what I think is going to start driving the next generation of attractions.”

Acknowledging how quickly tech can become obsolete, Valastro agrees that guests must remain at the centre of every experience, and notes that technology and design ideas should ultimately revolve around the audience and the emotions.

Creativity at the sector’s core

Concluding the session, Baskerville asked what challenges Forrec and Moment Factory are currently facing.

Kim says that for Forrec, it is keeping technology in check.

“Because it's evolving at such a lightning speed, it's easy to let technology drive the experience.

“The real challenge is making sure that technology is a tool to help serve our stories, the emotions, and the guests. We need to make sure that imagination always stays front and centre.”

Drawing on her film and television background, Valastro says that the trend of revisiting past successes, such as older movies, is making creativity very fragile.

These successes are proven and data-backed, while new innovations are risky and demand effort, uncertainty, and budget. But it is these innovations that drive the sector's incremental evolution.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by MOMENT FACTORY (@momentfactory)

“So one of our challenges is making sure that we're constantly renewing our creative ideas, but it's also having guests, visitors, spectators, and clients open to exploring what could be next.”

“I think that's the biggest challenge,” she adds, “allowing ourselves to take those risks.”

title: Beyond the kiddie coaster
summary:
While theme and amusement parks have traditionally offered attractions for different age groups, operators are increasingly adding family rides that let different generations experience them together. Instead of watching while their young child rides, parents and grandparents can share the experience.

For operators, these attractions offer an opportunity to create shared experiences for families visiting together, allowing children and adults to experience the same attraction rather than being separated by height or age requirements.

This has contributed to growing interest in family coasters and other attractions designed to appeal to a broad age range.

ART Engineering, Lagoon Amusement Park and Potts Park offer examples of how ride engineering, operator-manufacturer collaboration and accessibility are influencing the development of family attractions.

​Opening coaster experiences to a wider demographic


For family attractions, minimum height requirements are an important consideration for operators and manufacturers.

Minimum height requirements are determined by factors including ride design, restraint systems, and applicable safety requirements, and they can determine which family members can ride together. Many coasters require riders to be at least 100 cm, 110 cm or 120 cm tall, excluding young children eager to graduate from flat rides.

ART Engineering, which has been developing innovative roller coasters, dark rides, carousels, and water rides since its founding in Kirchzarten, Germany, in 2003, has made the 90 cm (32 inches) height requirement a cornerstone of its family portfolio.


By engineering a system that lets children measuring just 90 cm ride safely when accompanied by an adult, the company has opened its coaster experiences to an entirely new demographic.

Georg Behringer, managing director of ART Engineering, says operators are increasingly looking to create attractions that multiple generations can experience:


"Many of our clients focus on families as their target customers, aiming to provide a shared experience for family members of all ages. Our family roller coasters are designed according to that focus. The seats and restraint systems are suitable for small children and also offer comfortable accommodation for large adults.

“Combined with a dynamic—though not overly aggressive—ride experience, this ensures a fantastic time for all ages"

Designing a vehicle and restraint system that can securely accommodate both a child and an adult presents a significant engineering challenge. The physical differences mean that a lap bar fitting snugly against an adult's thighs could create a hazardous gap over a child's lap.

To overcome this, ART Engineering has developed seating and restraint systems designed to accommodate a wide range of rider sizes, including systems that close from above or secure the lap individually, adapting dynamically to different body shapes and sizes without sacrificing passenger comfort.

"We put a great deal of effort into developing the seat,” says Behringer. “The goal was to ensure that both small passengers and large adults could sit safely and comfortably. To achieve this, we conducted extensive tests with a wide range of people.

“The result is that a baseball player can now ride our roller coasters together with their three-year-old child."

​Braus & Saus at Potts Park


For Potts Park, a family-oriented amusement park in Minden, Germany, introducing a roller coaster that could cater to very young children while still offering an exciting ride experience was a key goal. The result was Braus & Saus, a custom-designed Family Shuttle Launch Coaster from ART Engineering.


Park owner Henrik Pott explains that the decision of manufacturing partner came down to trust and a willingness to iterate on the design:

"A key reason to choose ART is the relationship of trust involved in the collaboration. For our roller coaster, ART kept iterating the layout until we had the best solution. We recall going through eight different versions. The Wild Stone Age themed area found its fitting finale with the Braus & Saus attraction.

"The ride’s alignment with the heartline is superb, making the entire experience a real pleasure."

Repeated design iterations allowed the teams to refine the layout and the forces riders experience. The track is designed around riders' centre of gravity (the "heartline"). This alignment ensures that transitions, banks, and curves are smooth, eliminating lateral jolts and jerks that could otherwise scare or discomfort a young child.


In a park where families with young children are the primary demographic, offering a high-speed, dynamic-launch coaster for families is a significant competitive advantage.

"Most of our attractions are accessible to children from three years of age when accompanied by an adult. Beyond that, many guests are impressed that Braus & Saus is also open to riders from three years of age,” says Pott.

Pott says the combination of the ride experience and theming has also contributed to its appeal:

"Visitors are absolutely delighted with Braus & Saus. Feedback has been universally positive, with many guests immediately getting back in line for another ride. People particularly highlight the "farting" mammoths and the ride's smooth operation."

The success of Braus & Saus shows that a family coaster is not just about the physical track, but about the storytelling and the joy it brings. "Ultimately, the overall storytelling and its execution determine an attraction's success. It is difficult to point out just one element.

“What we value most about working with ART is our shared commitment to creating the best possible product and their availability to make necessary optimisations even after the ride has launched."

Primordial at Lagoon


Meanwhile, at Lagoon Amusement Park in Farmington, Utah, the same focus on family audiences was applied on a much larger scale with Primordial, an award-winning interactive coaster and dark ride hybrid.

In 2023, Lagoon opened this themed, interactive family coaster, representing one of the most ambitious engineering undertakings in the park's history. It features a custom-built mountain, interactive shooting elements, slow-moving dark ride sections with rotating gondolas, and sudden drops.


Dustin Allen, Lagoon's director of engineering, says that Primordial filled a spot in the park’s attraction lineup that was missing, adding: “The guest reception has been fantastic, with queue lines today continuing to prove the ride’s popularity three years after opening.

“In fact, Lagoon had to alter the park opening to accommodate the number of guests going directly to Primordial at “rope drop”, as well as changing ride operation closing policies to support the popularity of the ride."

Allen details the collaborative spirit that made ART Engineering a good fit for the ambitious project:

"The design, manufacture, installation, and commissioning of Primordial required very intricate communication and coordination. Relationships with the several companies involved in the project were crucial to the success of the ride.

“Lagoon has partnered with ART Engineering for several projects throughout the years (including the Cannibal and Bombora rides), and that relationship of trust and cooperation was solid.”

Primordial represented an evolution of the interactive coaster concept.

Although ART Engineering had previously developed similar dark ride/coaster hybrid technology for Canada's Wonderland with the Wonder Mountain's Guardian attraction, the concept for Primordial was developed further through new train designs, interactive targeting, and additional physical coaster elements.

“ART Engineering had proven to be more than capable of tackling these challenges and did so with distinction.”


Allen says the attraction has also had an impact on Lagoon's attendance:

“Park attendance has grown each year since the announcement of that ride. Many comments have been received about the upgrades to the amusement park in recent years, with Primordial being a prime example of Lagoon going above and beyond the expectations of the guests in providing world-class rides and attractions.”

Additionally, Primordial received multiple national and international recognitions, including an IAAPA Brass Ring Award, USA Today Reader’s Choice Award, and placing in blooloop’s Innovation Awards.

The recognition has also helped attract visitors from outside the local region, he adds:

"Primordial changed both the landscape (figuratively and literally, we built a mountain for this ride!) and the perception of what Lagoon – a regional park in Utah – is able to provide as an experience for our guests."

​​From kiddie coasters to new adventures


One of ART Engineering's greatest strengths is its diversified family ride portfolio. Its range includes traditional lift coasters alongside launch, shuttle, and interactive concepts, allowing operators to choose different ride formats based on available space and the desired experience.

At the entry level is the Kiddie Coaster, designed specifically for the youngest riders. This model, a gentle introduction to coaster kinetics, can be found at leading theme parks such as Europa-Park in Germany and Legoland Windsor in the UK.


The classic Family Coaster is the company's signature model. Featuring either a traditional chain lift or a friction wheel lift, this coaster incorporates thrilling, family-friendly track elements while utilising a low FRP (fibre-reinforced plastic) shell so children over 90 cm have a clear, unobstructed view from every seat.

This classic model has been installed at parks like Nigloland in France.

The portfolio has also expanded into launch and shuttle formats, including the Family Launch Coaster, Family Spike Launch Coaster and Family Shuttle Launch Coaster. These designs introduce acceleration and changes in direction while retaining the lower height requirements associated with family attractions.


Family Coaster from 90cm height restriction:

  • Kiddie Coaster
  • Family Coaster
  • Family Launch Coaster
  • Family Shuttle Launch Coaster
  • Family Spike Launch Coaster incl. switch track
  • Family Duelling Launch Coaster (coming in 2027)
  • Family Thrill Coaster

Controlled rotating coaster (4 seats in a row):

  • Adventure Coaster
  • Adventure Interactive Coaster

Coaster with inversions:

  • Mega Coaster


At the start of 2026, ART Engineering relaunched its Adventure Coaster product category. Building on the lessons of interactive ride engineering, the Adventure Coaster represents a step forward in personalised storytelling. It debuted as the Galacticoaster at Legoland Florida and Legoland California.

Galacticoaster also illustrates the shift towards more interactive coaster experiences, with riders able to configure their digital spacecraft before boarding.


"The feedback has been consistently positive,” says Behringer.

“The Legoland Galacticoaster combines a fantastic ride experience with show effects. Riders are immersed in the story right from the queueing area. This approach creates a personalised experience for the rider, going beyond mere theming."

The Adventure Coaster uses four-seat vehicles and a central boarding platform, a layout designed to keep groups together during the experience.

​Across the thrill spectrum


While family-friendly attractions are a major focus for ART Engineering, the company’s engineering capabilities also extend to extreme thrills, for example, the iconic Cannibal mega coaster at Lagoon.

"Cannibal is the result of close collaboration with Lagoon,” says Behringer. “The goal was to create a unique roller coaster offering intense thrills and inversions.”

Opened in 2015, Cannibal features an enclosed vertical tower lift, a 110-degree nose-dive drop, and the high-speed Lagoon Roll inversion.


Allen adds: "Cannibal really put Lagoon on the map. Bombora [a custom family coaster] was the first collaborative coaster with ART Engineering and set the stage for the ambitious Cannibal, Lagoon’s second collaborative coaster. Cannibal became the tallest and fastest ride in the park when it opened.

“With the unique tower lift system, it also became an iconic landmark for the park. It is loved by guests for its smooth track, unique elements, and consistently moving queue line (the ride regularly hits the theoretical capacity of 1200 PPH).

“Possibly Cannibal’s greatest attribute is the operational uptime and consistency. Through the first ten seasons of operation, the ride was able to open each day that the park opened. There were days that the ride was operational only for a short time, but there was never a full day where guests were left without the opportunity to ride the marquee attraction."

Cannibal's operational record also highlights the importance of reliability and long-term performance alongside ride design and engineering.

​Long-term reliability with ART Engineering


For operators making a multi-million-dollar investment in a new coaster, long-term reliability is as important as the initial ride experience. When an attraction is out of service, guest satisfaction falls, queue times at other rides lengthen, and the park's overall reputation suffers.


Behringer says ART considers long-term operation during design and development, supported by post-launch service.

"The customer invests in a product intended for long-term use. ART Engineering's goal is to deliver quality. To achieve this, the product's lifespan requirements are considered throughout the development process. Careful component selection, comprehensive quality management, and our ongoing service are prerequisites for a successful product lifespan."

An extensive parts & service programme underpins this dedication to quality.

Looking ahead, Behringer expects family coaster designs to continue developing.

“I think family roller coasters will continue to evolve—with new ride elements, more extensive theming, and greater customisation,” says Behringer. “New manufacturing processes are being implemented, and AI may increasingly play a role in certain processes."

​The evolution of the family coaster


The examples of Potts Park and Lagoon illustrate how the family coaster category is expanding beyond traditional children's attractions, with operators and manufacturers exploring lower height requirements, more sophisticated ride systems, and greater interactivity.


For operators considering a next-generation family coaster, Henrik Pott's advice is to start with the intended audience and the fit between the attraction and the park:

"Pay attention to your target audience and ensure the ride is a good fit for them. If the ride has already been installed elsewhere, try it out for yourself."

As the distinction between family and thrill attractions becomes less defined, the family coaster category is likely to continue evolving. For operators, the challenge is not simply to lower the minimum height requirement, but to create an experience that works for different ages, confidence levels, and expectations within the same attraction.

Attendees at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026, taking place in London from 22 - 24 September, can meet the ART Engineering team at booth #S803, where they can learn more about the company's roller coaster projects.

title: Attractions.io partners with Bosque de Chapultepec on new guest app
summary:
Attractions.io, a leading creator of mobile visitor apps, has partnered with Bosque de Chapultepec, a vast park in Mexico City that includes nine museums, a castle, and a zoo. Together, the organisations have developed a new app that helps guests explore the 866-hectare site.

At almost three times the size of Central Park, Bosque de Chapultepec is often best approached as a collection of attractions, with several visits needed to simply see the highlights.

Visitors at Bosque de Chapultepec can explore multiple atttractions across four different sectionsImage courtesy of Attractions.io

In a site this vast, wayfinding tools and staff can only do so much to point visitors toward their chosen attractions, let alone reveal the park's hidden corners.

As such, the park needed a unified digital experience that could orient visitors across all four of its sections in real time, even with limited phone signal.

This experience needed to help visitors plan their day based on their interests and available time, discover what's on (including exhibitions, events, and seasonal activities), and reach visitors directly with updates, reducing the reliance on physical signage.

The resulting app helps guests navigate the complex site with confidence, garnering 30,000 downloads per month and a 4.9-star rating on the App Store.

Data-backed decision-making

The team partnered with Attractions.io to create a brand-new mobile app that uses interactive maps and GPS wayfinding to help visitors move between sections and surface points of interest, facilities, and food options as they explore.


Aldair Contreras, digital manager, Bosque de Chapultepec, says: "We have hundreds of activities, but they're often not in a fixed location; they might be in the forest or out on the grass.

"Having accurate points of interest has helped our guests find activities more easily, as well as helping them discover new experiences they didn't know about when they arrived."

More than 150 unique activities are now discoverable and promoted through the app. These range from historic monuments to free activities such as yoga sessions or watercolour workshops, many of which had never appeared on a printed map.

Data from the app also informs which activities are recommended to visitors while on site. With these recommendations, guests can build a plan around their interests and the time they have available, which also reveals hidden attractions they might otherwise miss.

For example, following major investment, funfair attendance failed to grow as anticipated. The team found that the barrier to attendance was awareness rather than appeal, and is using the app to overcome this challenge.

"International guests didn't know we had a funfair, and locals didn't know it had reopened," says Natasha Uren Vázquez, executive director, Bosque de Chapultepec.

"Now we have the app, we're promoting it more, and attendance has been rising steadily."

Precise communications

In addition to enhancing the visitor experience, the app offers a live picture of how guests explore, and the data has become one of the park's core tools for deciding where to invest.

"The reports we get from our app management console have been so important in helping us plan and grow for the future," says Natasha Uren Vázquez, executive director, Bosque de Chapultepec.

"We now know that 60% of our guests spend most of their time at a single location and are looking into investing more to improve that specific space."

These findings helped support a funding application for the long-overdue refurbishment of the park's dining areas, with the app's user data providing evidence on how many visitors were using those spaces.


Guests can use the new Bosque de Chapultepec app to plan their visit around their own interests and availabilityImage courtesy of Attractions.io

Bosque de Chapultepec also plans to use the app for location-targeted advertising.

As a public body, the park has to be mindful of how often and when it reaches out to visitors. With the app, messages can be sent only to relevant visitors. This can alert nearby app users, for example, that a yoga class starts in ten minutes, rather than broadcasting to the entire audience.

This precision allows the park to directly promote free events and festivals to visitors, rather than relying on social and local media reach.

Recently, Attractions.io helped drive food and beverage revenue by introducing mobile food ordering at Chester Zoo, the UK's most-visited wildlife attraction.
